title: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In early periods of earth's history, when forms of life were fewer and simpler, the rate of organic change was probably slower, and at the first dawn of life it may have been extremely slow.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: During early periods of the earth’s history, when the forms of life were probably fewer and simpler, the rate of change was probably slower; and at the first dawn of life, when very few forms of the simplest structure existed, the rate of change may have been slow in an extreme degree.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion”; section “Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history”. Scope: life on earth across its whole history

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch14-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Phanerozoic portions can be analyzed with existing data. The first dawn of life, which is central to the strongest prediction, lacks adequate temporal and organismal resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate rates of phenotypic and taxonomic change per unit time in early versus later fossil intervals, correcting for sampling, and compare rates with reconstructed diversity and complexity. Lower early rates would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The earliest history of life has an exceptionally sparse and biased record.

Molecular and morphological rate estimates are not directly comparable.

Complexity and rate of organic change have competing definitions.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.68
analysis feasibility: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.52
data adequacy: 0.35
data existence: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rate-through-time methods exist and can be applied to Phanerozoic fossils and to molecular trees, which covers the later part of the history the claim is about. The earliest interval, which carries the strongest wording, is exactly where public data are weakest. Sampling can imitate a slow start, so a low early rate in current compilations would not cleanly confirm the biological claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate origination, extinction and morphological rates in successive intervals from the origin of life to the present, and test whether rates are lower in the earlier, taxonomically poorer intervals. The claim is confirmed if early intervals are slower after sampling correction, and refuted if early rates are as high as or higher than later ones once rock availability is controlled.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A poor early rock record produces the appearance of slow change even if the biological rate was high.

The first dawn of life, where the claim says change may have been extremely slow, has almost no fossil resolution of biological rates.

Molecular clocks pushed to the origin of life are dominated by the choice of model and calibration.
